rv.q: That may be why the lightness of the National Theater’s modern-dress “Hamlet,” on tour at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, is so discordant.
For a few halfhearted laughs they sacrifice the ability to make us care.
Hiran Abeysekera pulls out a charmingly cheeky yet heartbreakingly boyish Danish prince in Robert Hastie’s production of Hamlet from the National Theatre.

Hastie has not adopted the same approach for one of Shakespeare’s most popular tragedies. Abeysekera’s wry, animated performance, this “Hamlet” finds humor in its hero’s flaws and foibles, and those of other characters, without diminishing his struggle; the result is, while not one of the most harrowing renderings of this play I’ve seen, thoroug...
The ensemble is a wonderfully sharpened group of theater artists.
Unpersuasive as this Hamlet may ultimately be, there are only great things fated for Francesca Mills after this intrepid performance of Ophelia.
This “Hamlet” is often amusing, sometimes hilariously so, but it is rarely tragic.
Of course, Hamlet remains fascinating all by its 426-year-old self and as somebody remarks, the play’s the thing, and the National Theatre capably serves it here.
This is a play that, ambitiously, wants to embrace both the noble and the normal.
Individual moments register, but they don’t always connect.

cn.t: This National Theatre production delivers visual flair and a strong ensemble, but critics are divided on Hiran Abeysekera's unconventional, high-energy take on the melancholy Dane, with his idiosyncratic vocal choices proving polarizing.

vr.q: the performances were overall really great and this is definitely a production worth seeing
